incidents.title: User updates profile and refreshes immediately
incidents.brief: The primary database accepts a profile update, but a read goes to a replica that is still stale.
incidents.constraint: Replication is asynchronous and users expect freshness.
incidents.question: What keeps the experience correct?

choices.label: Fresh reads
choices.resultBody: Read-your-own-writes logic for that user or a short freshness window on their reads.

choices.label: Block all reads
choices.resultBody: Blocking reads until replication catches up stalls all 4,000 req/s, not just the writer's refresh; p95 climbs to 1 s and 40 requests error out.

choices.label: Disable replicas
choices.resultBody: The writer now sees fresh data, but all 4,000 req/s land on the primary; p95 stays near 880 ms and 20 requests error while its connection pool queues.

hints: The writer expects their own update.

choices.label: Fresh reads
choices.resultBody: Read the author’s writes from the primary or a fresh path.

choices.label: Force all reads
choices.resultBody: The next read still hit a lagging replica.

choices.label: Use CDN caches
choices.resultBody: Use CDN caches for everything

incidents.title: Comment count goes 41, 38, 41 on refresh
incidents.brief: Threadly's mobile app spreads each GET across 3 replicas lagging 0.2 s, 1.5 s and 9 s. On hot threads, replies appear, vanish and reappear as users refresh.
incidents.constraint: Replicas must keep serving 60k reads/s; the primary cannot absorb them.
incidents.question: What stops one user's view from going backwards in time?

choices.label: Pin each session to one replica via consistent hash

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Monotonic reads per session; staleness itself is unchanged.

choices.resultBody: Each session now hashes to one replica, so successive reads never jump to an older snapshot; rewinds fall from 7% to about 0.1%, mostly during replica failover. Cost: load spreads less evenly, and users pinned to the 9 s replica still see older, though monotonic, data.

choices.label: Route every read to the primary database
choices.resultBody: The primary was sized for writes plus replication, not 60k reads/s. Its CPU pegs at 98%, p95 jumps to 1.4 s, and write latency degrades for every user.

choices.label: Put a 30-second CDN cache in front of reads
choices.resultBody: The cache hides churn between refreshes, but each 30 s refill pulls from a random replica; when a refill lands on the 9 s-lag one, the count still jumps backwards for every user on that POP.

hints: The data eventually converges; the problem is the order users see it in.
Consecutive refreshes can land on replicas with very different lag.
What if one user's reads always followed the same replication stream?

choices.label: Read replicas
choices.resultBody: Pin the author’s reads to a fresh source or show a monotonic client-side count until replicas catch up.

choices.label: Show replica counts
choices.resultBody: The next read still hit a lagging replica.

choices.label: Stop counting likes
choices.resultBody: Stop counting likes

incidents.title: Two tabs save, one edit silently vanishes
incidents.brief: On Wikidocs, 3% of page saves overwrite a concurrent edit. Both tabs read version 17, edit, and write the whole page back; the later write wins and nobody is warned.
incidents.constraint: Editing sessions last up to 10 minutes, so holding locks while a page is open is not acceptable.
incidents.question: What makes the second save notice it is based on stale data?

choices.label: Compare-and-set on the version number, 409 on mismatch

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Optimistic concurrency: no locks, but conflicts surface to users.

choices.resultBody: The second save's UPDATE ... WHERE version = 17 now matches zero rows, so the API returns 409 and shows a merge view; lost edits drop from 3% to 0. Cost: about 3% of saves need a manual merge, and every client must send the version it read.

choices.label: Pessimistic row lock held while the page is open
choices.resultBody: Locks held through 10-minute editing sessions pile up; 18% of page opens now wait or time out, and abandoned tabs keep pages locked until the 15-minute lease expires.

choices.label: Last-write-wins using tightly synchronized server timestamps
choices.resultBody: Tighter clocks only make it more predictable which save wins; the losing tab's changes are still discarded without a warning, so 3% of saves keep vanishing.

hints: Nothing crashed; one write simply replaced another.
Both writers based their change on version 17.
Make the write succeed only if the row is still what the writer read.

incidents.title: Two workers both think they own the ledger lock
incidents.brief: Ledgerly's billing worker froze 14 s in a GC pause. Its 10 s lease expired, a second worker took over, then the first woke up and kept writing. 212 invoices double-posted.
incidents.constraint: Leases stay; the ledger database is the only place both writers meet.
incidents.question: What stops the stale lock holder's writes from landing?

choices.label: Fencing token per lease; ledger rejects lower tokens

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Safety moves to the storage layer; clients must propagate tokens.

choices.resultBody: Each lease grant carries an increasing token (33, then 34), and the ledger refuses any write tagged lower than the highest it has seen, so Worker A's post-pause writes fail. Cost: every write path must carry the token, and storage needs a conditional-write check.

choices.label: Shorten the lease TTL from 10 s to 3 s
choices.resultBody: A 14 s GC pause still outlives a 3 s lease, and ordinary network blips now trigger spurious failovers; double-posts only drop to 150 while leader churn triples.

choices.label: Have each worker recheck its lease before writing
choices.resultBody: Worker A checks, sees a valid lease, then stalls before its write lands; the check-then-act gap still lets 180 invoices double-post, because the ledger has no idea the lease moved.

hints: The first worker never learned it had been replaced.
Any check the worker makes itself can go stale during a pause.
The ledger needs a way to tell an old lock holder from a new one.

incidents.title: Quote screens show prices up to 40 s old
incidents.brief: TradeLite serves 120k quote reads/s from 6 async replicas. Lag is usually 300 ms, but during a bulk import two replicas fall 40 s behind and customers trade on stale prices.
incidents.constraint: The contract caps quote staleness at 2 s, and the primary cannot serve 120k reads/s.
incidents.question: How do you enforce the 2 s bound without moving reads to the primary?

choices.label: Pull replicas lagging more than 2 s out of routing

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Bounded staleness by exclusion; capacity drops while replicas catch up.

choices.resultBody: The router polls replication lag every 250 ms and drains any replica past 2 s; stale-quote reads fall from 31% to about 0.3%. Cost: four replicas now carry all 120k reads/s at 86% CPU, so you need headroom or a seventh replica.

choices.label: Add two more async replicas to spread load
choices.resultBody: The two new replicas replay the same bulk import and fall 35 s behind as well; the router still sends them a share of traffic, so 30% of reads remain over the 2 s bound.

choices.label: Cache quotes in Redis with a 5-second TTL
choices.resultTitle: The cache breaks the SLA by itself
choices.resultBody: A 5 s TTL alone can serve quotes older than the 2 s bound, and cache fills from the 40 s-behind replicas lock stale prices in; over-bound reads rise to 38%.

hints: Most replicas are fine; a couple are far behind.
The SLA is about the age of the data, not the speed of the response.
Decide per replica, based on how far behind it currently is.

incidents.title: Cart forgets the item added seconds ago
incidents.brief: ShopNest's cart store keeps N=3 replicas with W=1 writes and R=1 reads for speed. After a node blip, 4% of cart reads miss an item added seconds earlier.
incidents.constraint: Reads and writes must both keep working with one replica down; there is no single leader.
incidents.question: Which quorum setting guarantees a read sees the latest acknowledged write?

choices.label: Write quorum W=2 and read quorum R=2 with N=3

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Overlapping quorums trade a few ms of latency for read-after-write.

choices.resultBody: With R + W = 4 > N = 3 on strict (not sloppy) quorums, every read set shares at least one replica with the last acknowledged write, and one node can still fail. Missing items drop to about 0; cost: p95 rises from 12 ms to 19 ms waiting for the second replica.

choices.label: Write W=3 to all replicas, keep reads at R=1
choices.resultTitle: Writes fail whenever a node dips
choices.resultBody: R=1 plus W=3 does overlap, but every write now needs all three replicas; during the next 90 s node restart every add-to-cart fails, breaking the one-node-down requirement.

choices.label: Keep R=1, W=1 and retry reads that look empty
choices.resultBody: A cart missing one item is not empty, so the retry rarely fires; when it does, it asks another single replica that may also be behind. Misses only fall from 4% to 3.5%.

hints: Each write is acknowledged after reaching just one of three replicas.
A single-replica read may pick a different node than the write did.
Make the nodes you read from always intersect the nodes you wrote to.
